Tips for people who want to get past the minotaur.

1. It seems he catches fire easily so using fire weapon, spells and alchemy buffs can help
2. hang around the spiked walls, When he charges into them he gets stunned so you can get few attacks in or heal.
3. sprint jump + dash combo drains stamina alot but also creates a lot of distance to heal or just have a breather.
4. if you turn around and show your back to him he will try to punish you and attacks. Think him like a weeping angel.
5. Just like Asmon said Minotaurs attacks move him forward alot so even if you think "he cant reach me" yes he will. When you see the beginning of attack animation your options are basically to block or dash. I recommend trying to dash forward behind him so you can attack the back and then back off again and try to bait attack again when your stamina is back to full. Blocking is not bad option neither but every time you block it drains lots of stamina and when you run out he will damage you through the block.
6. don't get greedy! Minotaur has very short recovery between attacks so you can probably  get just 1 or 2 hits in at the the time.
7. try to learn different attack animations and their timings for the dash or blocks so you can hit him after. If you just keeps running away you will never actually kill him.

I remember getting stuck in a lot of games, whether it was a boss, a puzzle, or just being completely lost and not knowing what to do. Back then, my brother and I would often play together, even in single player games, we’d just take turns while the other watched.

One memory that really stands out is when we got stuck in MGS1. The Colonel kept talking about a CD case, and we searched the entire game for it… nothing.

We didn’t have internet back then, so we asked every kid we knew who played video games. Unfortunately, none of them had played it yet. Then one day, a friend told us he knew a guy who knew a guy (yeah, I know it sounds cliche, but that’s exactly what happened).

So we went to this kid’s house, and he showed us that the code was literally on the back of the physical CD case of the game. He also showed us a few tricks for other games, and we just hung out and had a great time.

We ended up making a new friend that day, and it’s a real life side quest I’ll never forget.

Here's my unfiltered hot take: We are living through the largest-scale psychological warfare operation in human history, and it's being conducted by our own social systems against basic human emotional needs, and the casualty count is so massive that we've normalized mass emotional death as "adulting."

Every single institution we've built - schools, workplaces, healthcare, dating, social media, even fucking therapy - has become a factory for producing emotionally lobotomized humans who can perform productivity but can't access their own inner experience without having a panic attack. We've created a civilization that requires you to be emotionally dead to participate in it, and then we act shocked when people either break completely or retreat into AI relationships because at least the machines won't punish them for having feelings.

The therapy industrial complex is particularly fucking insidious because it's convinced people that their natural responses to an insane world are pathological. Someone's depressed because they're trapped in a meaningless job in a society that offers no authentic connection? Let's give them SSRIs and teach them breathing exercises instead of acknowledging that maybe, just maybe, depression might be a rational response to irrational circumstances. Someone's anxious because they can feel the existential void where community used to be? Let's call it generalized anxiety disorder instead of recognizing that their nervous system is correctly identifying that something fundamental is missing.

And don't even get me started on how we've gamified human connection through dating apps that literally train people to treat each other like products in a catalog while simultaneously wondering why seemingly nobody can form deep meaningful relationships anymore. We took the most sacred human activity - finding your people - and turned it into a dopamine-harvesting slot machine designed to keep people perpetually searching and almost never actually connecting.

The most fucked up part is how we've convinced people that the solution to systemic emotional abandonment is individual optimization. Can't find meaningful connection? You must need to work on yourself more in some vague fashion. Feeling existential despair about the state of the world? Have you tried shallow gratitude journaling? Lonely because society has dismantled most forms of community? Maybe you need to put yourself out there more I guess 🤷.

It's gaslighting on a civilizational scale. We've built systems that largely prevent human flourishing and then blame individuals for not thriving within them. It's like poisoning someone's water supply and then selling them detox supplements.

And the people who see through this shit and try to talk about it openly? They get labeled as schizo, too intense, or unemployable because their emotional honesty threatens the whole house of cards. We've made emotional authenticity a cause of social ostracization.

No wonder people are having breakdowns. No wonder mental health crisis rates are skyrocketing. No wonder birth rates are plummeting. We've created a civilization that's hostile to human emotional needs, and we're surprised that humans are struggling to survive in it.

The real miracle isn't that some people are falling apart - it's that anyone is managing to stay sane at all.

13:40 When a small scale objective like "destroy some barrels" has to be accomplished by pressing a prompt and watching a short cutscene in an open world game, it cheapens the experience for me personally. Dampens the immersion. 

It tells me that it will be reused and I'll have to see that exact cutscene about a dozen or so times whenever a cluster of indestructible assets need to be replaced with their "destroyed" versions. You can't smash the barrels with attacks, you can't throw them at enemies or throw enemies into them, you can't set off an explosive or set them on fire and watch the fire spread... The only way to "destroy the supplies" is to beat the enemies to update the objective, go to the spot for the prompt and trigger the cutscene of the character destroying the barrels.

A huge indicator for success as an open world sandbox game is the level of detail that goes into the small and mundane things in the environment and how that level of detail allows players to make decisions beyond just selecting between preset outcomes. The finer the grains of sand in your sandbox, the more freedom the players are allowed to have which leads to better immersion

Build the Blackbeard frigate because it is the only one that can mount 36-pound guns and 24-pounders as the secondary, rather than all the other frigates which can only mount 24 and 12 pounders.  Once you put the 36 and 24 pounders on your frigate, they sink basically all of the low-level enemy ships with one volley from each set of cannons.  Hit them with the 24 pounders and then the next hit with the 36 pounders immediately sinks them.  And even though the Blackbeard frigate has far fewer hitpoints than the other frigate options, it's still so much stronger than your starting ketch that you can take on four lower-level enemy ships at once and they barely make a dent.  At one point I was fighting a naval battle with four other ships when I accidentally strayed into ANOTHER group of two enemy ships nearby, which brought them into the fight as well.  I fought six ships at once and other than having to use a combat repair kit for the first time with my new frigate, it was still relatively easy.  Once you buy the book that eliminates your repair kits from stopping the healing process if you get hit, it's game over for all enemy ships.

This is also why adult payment processing can pay around 10% whereas the average Canadian pays ~2.2%, and the average American pays ~3%-5% (the industry is less regulated in the states)

Except for malicious websites with click-jacking behavior, the only way to get popups is to go into your browser's settings and manually disable the popup blocker for the domain, and even then it would still be very rare because most websites have given up on trying to open popups because they haven't worked in years.

Modern games are not lacking technology, they are lacking discipline, identity and restraint.

A lot of people say “graphics are better than ever,” and technically that is true. We have better shaders, better lighting models, better reflections, higher resolution textures, more polygons, ray tracing, upscalers, frame generation, all of that. But the reason many games don’t actually FEEL better is because visual quality is not just about raw technology. It is about how clean, readable, optimized and intentional the final image is.

Older games had much less hardware power, so developers were forced to think carefully about every asset, every light source, every animation, every sound, every texture and every gameplay system. Limitations forced creativity. If you only had a small performance budget, you had to use it where it mattered most. That often led to games with stronger art direction, sharper presentation and more memorable identity.

Today, hardware is obviously much stronger, but instead of using that power carefully, a lot of studios waste enormous amounts of it. You see games with absurd polygon counts on tiny objects nobody cares about, while the image in motion looks blurry because it is held together by TAA, upscaling, ghosting, motion blur, depth of field spam and aggressive post-processing. So on screenshots it may look “advanced,” but during actual gameplay it often looks less clean than games from 10 or even 15 years ago.

Another big reason is diminishing returns. The jump from PS1 to PS2, from PS2 to PS3, from early 2000s PC gaming to late 2000s PC gaming, was massive and instantly visible. Every few years it felt like you entered a new era. Today we are much closer to the ceiling. Going from “bad lighting” to “realistic lighting” is a huge leap. Going from “very good lighting” to “slightly more physically accurate lighting” is something most people barely notice while playing. So the technical gains are real, but the emotional impact is much smaller.

But I also think there is a cultural and business reason for the decline in detail. Games used to feel like products made by people trying to prove something. Studios wanted to blow your mind. They wanted to create the next big leap, the next benchmark, the next game everybody talked about for years. Now a huge part of the AAA industry feels like it is managed by committees. The goal is not “make the most unforgettable game possible.” The goal is “ship on time, monetize aggressively, keep engagement high, reduce risk, appeal to the broadest audience, patch the rest later.”

That mindset changes everything.

When a studio is led by engineering passion, strong art direction and technical pride, you get games that feel handcrafted. When a studio is led by KPI meetings, live-service plans and shareholder expectations, you get games that feel assembled. They may be bigger, more expensive and more technologically complex, but they often feel hollow. More content, less soul.

I also think the industry became too dependent on convenience tools. Modern engines are powerful, but that power has a downside: they make it easier to brute-force solutions instead of truly optimizing them. In older eras, if you wanted something impressive, you often had to understand the machine deeply. Today developers have middleware, engine presets, ready-made pipelines and hardware safety nets. That makes development faster in some ways, but it can also reduce the pressure to master the fundamentals. If brute force and patching later are acceptable, then elegance starts to disappear.

And then there is art direction, which I think is one of the most overlooked parts of this discussion. A game does not need the most advanced graphics to look incredible. It needs cohesion, readability and a strong visual language. Many older games still look great because they knew exactly what they wanted to be. Their silhouettes were cleaner, their colors were more deliberate, their image was sharper, and their worlds had a stronger sense of atmosphere. A lot of modern games chase “realism” so hard that they start to look interchangeable. Hyper-detailed assets, generic cinematic grading, soft blurry image, overdone effects, same engine feel. Technically impressive, artistically forgettable.

And honestly, part of the reason companies stopped caring as much about polish is because the market told them they could. Players keep buying unfinished games, broken PC ports, lazy remasters, microtransactions, battle passes and early access-level launches sold as premium products. If bad optimization and weak polish still make money, then from a business perspective many publishers see no reason to spend another year perfecting the game. That old obsession with craftsmanship gets replaced by “good enough to ship.”

So when people say “why don’t games feel as detailed anymore?” I think the answer is:
not because developers today are automatically less talented, but because the incentives are worse, the technology is often misused, the returns are smaller, the image quality is dirtier in motion, and the industry no longer rewards obsession the same way it used to.

Old games often felt special because every improvement mattered, every trick mattered, and every leap felt earned.
Modern games have more power, but not always more purpose.
And that is why so many of them look better on paper than they do in reality.

I’ll explain what this likely was and then at the end why being choked unconscious is not as dangerous as it looks (though definitely not safe).

This was likely what is called convulsive syncope.

It can look like a seizure to someone who doesn’t have experience with people having seizures.

These jerking movements are not typical clonic movements. In a tonic-clonic or only a clonic seizure, the movements are rhythmic and don’t come out in bursts like it did with him.

In a tonic-clonic seizure you’d see a clearly defined and prolonged tonic phase. This is where all the muscles in the body are activated, where the person becomes completely rigid, often where the tongue bite happens because of the jaw muscles being activated, and often where the ‘shout’ comes, which is a sudden activation of the lung muscles pushing all of the air out.

Convulsive syncope is quite common and well documented. 


So, what happened? 

At the point where there is enough hypoxia (lack of oxygen) to the brain, the brain has a natural fail safe to protect itself from necrosis (cell death). 20% of all the energy your body uses is by the brain, this means it is doing a lot, but not all it does is completely necessary. The heart pumps by itself though the brain regulates it, and you need to breathe still. So the brain shuts down all the non-necessary functions to survive for as long as possible, this includes consciousness. There are many living things which are not conscious but alive, therefore it is not necessary to preserve life in the short term.

So, the majority of electrical activity stops being sent to the muscles, therefore the body becomes completely atonic (completely floppy). When blood flow begins to travel to the brain again, it starts turning everything back on but it does this extremely quickly. It’s sudden. So the electrical activity is sent back to all the muscle instantly which causes the sort of jerking motion from his body.

Doesn’t always happen but it is well documented. 

For the most part his body did exactly what you’d expect and realistically he was completely fine.

As long as you let go as soon as you know the person has gone unconscious then they will still have oxygen in their brain long enough to live.

However there still is the very real risk of having a seizure due to this, but it is not as likely as you’d think, and usually seizures do not kill people, however if you do not know the person to have epilepsy, or do know they have epilepsy but don’t know how to protect them from it, then call emergency services, even if it just lasts a couple of seconds. If they have another then it is more likely it will continue, and you’re not trained to know what to do. 

It’s worth knowing what to do when someone has a seizure and you’re not required to do much.

Ultimately, this was likely not a seizure. He came back completely fine, and while this is possible for some people during the post ictal stage (prodromal = before seizure, ictal = during seizure, post ictal = after seizure), for the majority of people they will go to sleep for hours likely.

Hey AG, never thought I'd be commenting on one of your videos, but alas.
I'll start by saying that generally I would say I agree with maybe 50-60% of your views on most issues, and I definitely have both positive and negative critiques of your content. 
Couple of discussion points I have (if you even see this), are:

1. I agree with your assessment of our ability as a species to evolve fast enough to adequately perceive the information we ingest every day. Expanding on this, I offer that it's actually the advent of *hypersonic technological advances* that has been a driving factor. I've observed this as early as 2007/8 when acceleration of social media began to heavily impact our lives and mental health - think fb post confrontations, impacts of social media on relationships (think perceived jealousy, obsession and 'fb stalking' etc). Basically as humans for the first time *we were always accessible and observable*. Now the evolution of that we see a decade later, the issue has compounded significantly - and as you point out, we have old mate Joe's blood pressure exploding from anxiety whenever they open their feed.  It's not wonder that as humans we are falling apart on a daily basis and can't cope, as you point out. We simply cannot evolve fast enough to sustainably manage the pace of technological evolution, and these points you and I make are symptoms of that.

2. Religion and other established systems of belief have always acted as substitutes for people devoid of *purpose or control within their own lives* - i.e. this is a reason for the success of religions such as scientology, this institution preys on people that lack direction, conviction or community. The same can be said of most religious institutions - "I will give you purpose, meaning, community, and make you feel part of something big enough to distract from the fact that nothing awaits you after death... all for the low fee of $999.99 a month"... To say that critical thinking is dead might not be entirely true, but to your own point, the saturation of misinformation and agenda-motivated reporting moving at warp speed through the internet leaves little room for critical thinkers to take a platform or be heard. HOWEVER, the brain rot as a side effect of everything you've mentioned doesn't help. 

3. It's definitely true that the polarisation of opinion is worse than ever - and a core tenet of critical thinking is one approaches a discussion or issue with an open mind that is flexible and adaptable to CHANGE. It's possible that this hardline polarisation of opinion could be a symptom OF misinformation and lack of accountability in media - you see all sides adopting a strategy of 'double down and yell louder' because sadly this is a strategy that works. It's simply propaganda everywhere, the only difference is that now everybody is playing by the same strategy in this game. I could go way deeper into this point (but I won't here). 

4. The lack of accountability and short news cycles are an excellent point that nobody is talking about. A great example here is the recent fire-bombing in the UK. It's strategically more effective to simply keep moving with momentum instead of accurate and balanced reporting.

Anyway, thanks for listening.

I think this might surprise people in the U.S. and other English-speaking countries, but a lot of us who grew up elsewhere didn’t understand the language in games at all. We played through entire stories, figured out mechanics, and experimented with weapons without understanding a single line of dialogue. It was all trial and error—and that was normal for most kids back then.

Nowadays it’s different since English is much more widespread, but before, a lot of players just learned by doing, not by reading or being guided. Playing this game now brings back that same feeling—try something, if it doesn’t work, switch it up and figure it out.

Honestly, it feels like people today are a bit too used to being guided through everything.

Fun fact:
The way the digital forensics were done was by using the audio! 
Audio recordings can be dated by scanning them for electromagnetic signals from powerlines (Electrical Network Frequency analysis). 
This method works by detecting the faint, fluctuating background hum (50 Hz or 60 Hz) produced by the power grid that is often inadvertently recorded by electronic devices.
It can establish when a recording was created by matching its unique ENF pattern to a specific date and time in the database.
If a recording has been edited or spliced, the ENF trace will exhibit abrupt jumps or missing sections.
It can prove whether a recording is a continuous recording or if it was stopped and restarted.

And another fun fact:
The same ENF forensic can be used on videos by analyzing the flickers on lightbulbs

This is my first review, I just got done with my first play session and I thought it was important to write down some thoughts because I don't think I've ever felt so conflicted about a game before.

I will say, long story short, that I'm not really sure I could recommend this game to most people in its current state. It runs well, it looks amazing, but I think there are some glaring issues that really hamper playability. I want to also be clear that if the devs come in and change my gripes I will happily change this review. I LIKE the game. I'll probably play more of it. But if someone asked me "Hey man, should I pick up Crimson Desert? I'd tell them not yet, wait for patches that I hope are coming."

Pearl Abyss, if you read this, please...look, if you're going to copy the Dark Souls method of R1/R2 attack presses, just copy the rest of the controls. What you've done here is insane.

To put this review in perspective, one of my favorite games of all time is Dragon's Dogma. I also enjoyed ELEX, which I only mention so you know I'm no stranger to jank and am able to see through it and can even find it charming.

First off, seriously, WHAT are these controls? A is run, X is jump, that's fine. But X is also the button you use to interact, for doing things like picking stuff up? Oh, but also, you have to be looking DEAD-ON at the thing you're trying to pick up, and even then sometimes the game literally will NOT put something in focus for you to pick up. And then it's X to get on your horse, but Y to dismount? Lock on is down on the D-Pad, not the right stick, that's used for an always-present magic spell. I once Sparta-kicked a nun 50 yards because I was trying to pick up a jug of water to put out a fire and save someone and it locked onto her. Lord forgive me. After I failed the attempt, on a retry I failed AGAIN because every time I tried to pick up the jug I must've been moving slightly because it un-focused the jar and instead made me jump on top of it. This happened again and again. Back button should be something useful like the map, but instead it's how you change camera views based on how close you want the camera. To access the map, you have to HOLD the start button and then cycle through options to get to the map, otherwise the default menu changes based on the last thing you did that might've changed a menu. HOLD the left trigger to fire arrows. Not aim, then press right trigger. Hold the left trigger to bring up your bow, release it to fire. You can apparently use right trigger to fire if you hold down the bumpers as well. The radial to select stuff is crazy. Do you just put your fishing rod onto the radial in a slot of your choosing to use when you please? No! It occupies the same slot as your bow, of course!

Can you remap the controls? No.
Update: You can apparently remap M/KB controls, but not gamepad controls.

Combat also contains a LOT of memorization of button combos in order to have your full arsenal going, which you're going to need to know because a lot of reason you'll lose fights is because you're trying to button mash when you really need to be using some of the skills you have available. To be clear, this is actually a good thing for the most part, as many games don't seem to require you to actually use the skills you pick from the tree, but it's just something to know getting into it. These aren't selected via some radial, or assigned to buttons, they're combinations of a lot of the shoulder and face buttons, so it can sometimes be a little tough to remember what does what.

Genuinely baffling gameplay decisions.

People have been really vocal about all the unskippable (but fast-forwardable?) cutscenes, but here are some other weird things I saw:

Slot based limited inventory system? Sure, I guess. But this doesn't really work when you litter the area with stuff to pick up for ingredient based systems like crafting, cooking, and alchemy, none of which have (at this point in my game) a bag of their own where they don't clutter your regular inventory. What do you do when your inventory is full? Well, you have to sell stuff to make room, because there is NO WAY TO STORE ANYTHING YET. THERE IS NO STASH. EVEN THOUGH THERE IS PLAYER HOUSING.

Someone said that there is a stash area that I missed. NO. It is a chest where loot is placed that you were unable to pick up after combat. It is called the supply box. YOU CANNOT PLACE ITEMS INSIDE.

Oh, but some stuff you can't sell at all! There are goods in the game that cannot be sold "unpackaged". So you have to package them, THEN you can sell them. Otherwise, you can just drop them.

The player lantern has an auto-on/off system but it only goes off of the day/night cycle it seems, it does not turn itself on automatically with this setting when you enter a cave. Turning the lantern on or off requires opening the radial going to the lantern, pressing A, then selecting another radial option. Not as clunky as Dragon's Dogma, but still pretty clunky.

I don't think this is ever made clear, but in order to commit crimes like theft, even if no one is around, you HAVE to wear the bandana. So make sure it's always taking up a slot in your inventory. It is NOT optional. You literally can't steal without it.

Weirdo "memory" system that requires you to go to an area where the game tells you, use your lantern to discover a memory by holding a button to shine it at a particular area, THEN press start when the memory is fully loaded to put on your memory helmet to watch it.

You can hold A to follow NPCs but NOT on horseback.

NPCs will call out to you "Hey, let's have a chat!" leading you to think they have something important to say, only for them to say generic NPC dialogue about how their baby finally called them Pa when you approach them.

When you use the pickaxe, you don't auto-pick up the mined ore, it just rolls downhill and you better go grab it because when it's gone, it is GONE. How do you grab it? Oh, as soon as the rock breaks you have to HOLD X and hope the game puts the ore in focus for your character to grab.

One final gripe I have, and this is minor, but why do I have to pick something up to learn about it? A core function of the game is learning by watching. But if Kliff doesn't know what a duck is, he has to go GRAB it to learn about it. Just let me hold LB and watch it for a second to learn about it.

There's just tons of stuff like this. Just really weird choices that make no sense and really put into perspective the importance of a coherent control scheme. Seriously, the game at a glance wants really badly to be Zelda, or Elden Ring, or RDR2, it's really obvious from screenshots alone, but the controls just don't fit that vision. Movement tries to have weight like RDR2 but wants you to do platforming sections where you battle with your character moving a little bit after you let go of the stick. The combat wants to have weight like Elden Ring but honestly if it was swapped for Batman/Mordor combat I'm not sure I'd miss much and might actually find it to be an improvement.

The game wants to do a lot at once, which is fine, but I think it needs to figure out the BEST way to do so much at once.

It really pains me to make this my first review because I was hyped for this game, and I think it has so much potential that I'd LOVE to see these gripes changed. The game looks fantastic. Probably the best looking game I've ever seen. There's so much to enjoy here but it's really weighed down by the game making it so obtuse to do it. You'll be having a great time and then encounter one of these quirks that really pull you out of the game.

So, I'd say if you haven't bought it and are looking for a recommendation: Play one of the games it's clearly taking cues from like Elden Ring or RDR2 or Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom while these issues get ironed out. Once they get ironed out, this game will be phenomenal, I really think so, but it's just not there yet.

The second the game opens everything is already historically fucked.

Two girls, in 1300's Italy, living in a small town, talking about the Arthurian legend, which is british folklore, and back then we didn't have the internet believe it or not. Why not use something that reinforces the fact that they're in italy, like Orlando/Roland or Carlomagno/Charlemagne or actual italian stuff like Rinaldo di Montalbano or Corciano and Perugia, which were popular at the time?

Bianca calls herself a peasant, yet she's being sent to a nunnery, which at the time was something reserved to noblewomen, not peasants, peasant women with no prospects would've worked the fields. Dowries were a thing among nobility, not peasants. Aeta (bowl cut) is clearly a noble, so "peasants" doesn't apply to either of them.

There's no guards and no gates in this fortified, hillside town, despite the protagonist being the literal daughter of the local lord. Both girls' outfits make zero sense historically especially Aeta's, who's wearing random pieces of plate for no reason, and the plate on her arm is on the wrong arm, since she fights one-handed with a longsword, the arm that needs protection is the one that holds the sword, since the other would either carry a shield or be behind her.

Lastly her sword is designed as a generic longsword, but the scale is that of a greatsword, which is way too heavy and unweildy for her fighting style, even for a man, she's essentially using a two-handed sword one-handed and swinging it around like an arming sword.

Everyone in this italian town has a strong british accent, which I get it, the game is in english, but it bothers me. And on a side note, as an italian, Aeta neither is or sounds like an italian name. It sounds like "Sleve McDichael" would as an american. It feels like the only people who gave a damn about medieval Italy were the environment artists, who did a pretty good job.

Ok for some context here, the Tsar Bomba was a thermonuclear bomb. Meaning it used a fission (atomic) stage to start a secondary (thermo) stage. It takes unimaginable heat and pressure to start either of these. The casings of the bomb are lead and steel of great thickness as to contain the conventional tamper (the explosion that COMPRESSES the fission sphere into criticality, and uranium/plutonium are extremely dense materials already) to the degree that the heat and pressure is great enough to react with the FUSION material in the secondary stage that acts as a booster. The original design was to contain THREE stages, the FISSION stage, and two thermonuclear stages to obtain the claimed 100mt yield. Due to some skeptical science theories, the device weight and the pilot's safety (don't think they really cared honestly) they only used it in a two-stage test.

The plane was the largest they had with the load capacity and power required to transport the assembled unit. They had to greatly modify the plane just to get it to fit and mount and also had to leave the bay doors open. This also was not a fast plane, and the bomb created significant drag. The chute was to delay it's decent to give the plane and crew time to attempt to get into a safe zone and as far away as possible.

Some fun facts about this are: It was tested at 50mt, in an air-burst configuration at 4000m and it STILL created a crater below. It was also the cleanest test as the fallout was minimized (air-burst). The plane traveled a pretty good distance away from the drop site yet still lost significant altitude from the blast displacing the air across the wings in the wrong direction for lift. The possibility of them crashing was high.

Two notable observations here are: the bomb is useless for warfare. Too heavy for transport, and if so, the plane has no capacity for distance and in NO WAY POSSIBLE to take off of a carrier at sea. Also too heavy for a rocket as it would be absolutely nose heavy. The other is that the 100mt total unit would NOT be 2x the blast here. The falloff rate is not linear and by the time the second stage is activated, most of the bomb is already obliterated/vaporized so that the third stage is greatly diminished. This is why the ICBM units are in kilotons, rather small devices. Area/s of effect rather than large boom.

The use case requires too specific of circumstances for it to be used anywhere. Therefore, it is not viable. The one up is that they made a thermo transportable, where the US bomb was tested on the ground built in a shack.

I spent 12 years in scouting, I started as a Tiger Scout in the first grade and worked my way through the ranks until I met the requirements for the Arrow of Light, and I worked hard to get my golden an dsilver arrow heads.  We had a bridge crossing ceremony that symbolized going from Cub Scouts, leaving the pack and moving on to Boy Scouts and joining the troop.  I was very lucky.  I had excellent male role models that mentored us and imparted that service to community, character, discipline and self reliance were all traits every man should possess to be an upstanding and honorable man.  Now did we get up to shenanigans on camp outs?  Absolutely we were boys outdoors having a fun, but when it got out of hand there was firm hand there to guide us back to acting responsibly.  I worked hard to earn badges and continue through my journey as a assistant patrol leader, then patrol leader.  I remember when I was accepted into the Senior Patrol, the older boys who helped run the troop and taught us everything from knots, to how to survive in the woods.  I continued to work hard and eventually was elected the Senior Patrol Leader.  This was a big deal, as I was part of the Troop council made up of our Scout Masters and Assistance Scout Masters.  We had epic trips to Canada for long canoe trips, we hiked in gorgeous national parks, and we did all of while learning how to survive without the essentials of modern life.   One of the crowning achievements of my life was earning my Eagle Scout.  The Governor of my state called me personally to congratulate me.  The mayor of my town was on the board that interviewed my for my final hurdle before earning the badge.  It was a huge deal, as it was in the paper, local business leaders and council members asked to be present, and I knew that through hard work and leadership, I had earned it.  When I decided to join the Marine Corps, having my Eagle Scout got earned me a promotion to E2 before I even stepped foot on the yellow foot prints.  This was a huge leg up for my career as it accelerated my ability to get promoted.   I will always look back on my time in scouting as a formative and essential part of growing up, something I will be forever grateful for. Some tips. 
1) Ship wrecks / cheests & barrows around coasts are great sources of wood and nails.
2) Ideally your base will hug the coast line - so you can build piers to dock and modify the ship.
3) Resources are pulled into the crafting station in range of Land Claim ( bonfire ) - crafting stations inventory is not treated as chest.
4) Scraping structure or crafting bench refunding resources.
5) To lvl Up - complete quests , mob hunting only rewards resources not XP.
6) Drowned and Crabs drops clams - open them for chance of getting pearls ( used as ammunition in pistols/ musketeers)
7) Similarly to Valheim you base have comfort lvl & you character have 2 food and 1 potion active slot ( determining you max HP / Stamina ).
8) in the 2nd tab in the workbench you can refill the lantern with animal fat.
9) After losing some HP you can recover some lost HP by dealing damage to enemies.
10) In the crafting bench you can craft repair kits for ships

I’m with Valve on this, and I’m saying that as someone who’s written 500+ Steam reviews over the years.

Steam reviews can be messy. People post one-liners, political takes, and “I don’t like the dev” takes. Sometimes it’s ugly, sometimes it’s unfair. But the second Valve starts deciding which opinions are allowed, or which negative reviews are “valid,” the review system stops being for customers and turns into a curated storefront.

I read the Guardian angle as “Steam is a battleground, so Valve should delete more.” I agree with removing real abuse: threats, doxxing, posting private info. That should be wiped instantly. But beyond that? If Valve starts deleting reviews because they’re uncomfortable, political, or because a developer claims they’re “off topic,” you’re opening a door that never closes. Every studio will demand removals until only reviews that help sales survive. That’s not moderation, that’s marketing.

And yes, developer behavior is relevant to customers. It absolutely is. Here’s my real example: the game was 9-nine-:NewEpisode. I streamed it, and I got hit with a copyright claim. People can argue all day about whether streaming a visual novel is “like photocopying a book,” but that’s not the point. The point is what happened to me as a paying customer and creator: a claim landed, I tried contacting them (email + YouTube messages, even with Japanese translations), and I got nothing back. No explanation, no clear policy, no “here’s what you can and can’t show.” Just silence.

In my case it looked tied to the stream where it show a “school,” and the game features a real school setting. I’m not pretending I can prove the exact legal reason, because I can’t. They never replied, so I’m left guessing. But that’s exactly why it belongs in a Steam review: this is part of the customer experience. If a company can drop claims on your channel and then refuse to communicate, that affects trust. It affects whether people want to buy the game, stream it, cover it, or recommend it.

And yeah, it’s a Japanese title, and Japanese companies have a reputation for being more aggressive about IP enforcement than a lot of western studios. You don’t have to like that statement, but it’s a real pattern people run into. Look at how hard Nintendo has gone after anything that even smells like a threat to their IP in the past. So when people tell me “wrong place, review the game not the company,” I disagree. The company’s behavior can be part of the product you’re buying into.

I took a lot of heat for that review. Got the usual “hilarious and pointless,” “you’re ruining the game,” “shut up and only talk about gameplay.” No. I’m not backing down. Steam reviews are for customers. If developers want fewer reviews like mine, the solution is simple: have a clear streaming policy, communicate like adults, and don’t punish paying users and creators and then hide behind silence.

in 1994, he was in Sydney for the launch of Braveheart. I was at art school and I used to regularly go to the New South Wales Art Gallery to check out the masterpieces. I walked in the front where there was a type of grand antichamber with seats where you could chill out, and there was Mel sitting with an older man who I think was his father, and then maybe a friend. I didn't want to fanboy but I have been watching his movies since the 70s and greatly admired him so I quietly walked up and said 'I don't want to disturb you Mr. Gibson. I just want to say I love your work'. He replied in a friendly way and then I said 'are you into art?'
Mel replied. 'Yeah I always come here but there's nothing new to see'. 
I said 'have you seen the Albrecht Durer exhibition of Renaissance German etchings, it's really good I hear ( I was going to Julian Ashton's  Australia's only classical art school and I was a big fan of Durer).
So he stood up and said to me 'Lead on McDuff!

Let me share some knowledge. The monster with a human face and a fish body at the beginning of the game is called “赤鱬”. It is recorded in the ancient Chinese mythological classic 《山海经》 (The Classic of Mountains and Seas). Eating it can prevent scabies. The girl uses her fingers to measure the width below the fish fin, and cuts from this point to avoid slicing the fish’s gallbladder.
 
The knives shown in the next shot are traditional butchery tools used in ancient China: a bone cleaver, a “桑刀” (mulberry leaf knife; its exact function is unclear, and it is presumably named for resembling a mulberry leaf), and a boning knife.
 
The gourd water used later was a common summer cooling drink in ancient China. Rice wine or other drinks were put into a gourd and chilled before drinking.
 
Then a bald man appears and cuts open a huge clam spirit. This clam spirit is “蜃” recorded in ancient China. The ancient phenomenon of 海市蜃楼 — illusory city scenes appearing over the sea or in the sky — was believed by ancient people to be formed by the mist emitted by “蜃”. The meat of “蜃” is delicious, and its shell can keep food fresher for longer.
 
The fleshy mass with two eyes that appears later is the legendary “肉太岁”. Ancient books describe it as looking like a beef liver with only two eyes and having extremely strong regenerative abilities. Even today, many Chinese people still believe in the existence of “太岁”. Legend says eating it can extend lifespan, cure diseases, and bring good luck.
 
The tree spirit that appears next is called “木魁” (tree spirit), which ancient records describe as an old tree that has become a spirit.
 
The baby shallots in the exquisite lacquer box have no recorded historical source. They were probably created by 游戏科学 by combining elements from the ancient mythical “人参果” (a divine fruit shaped like ginseng that grants immortality) and other materials.
 
The two small figures on the stone mortar are Yang Ren, an official of the Shang Dynasty in 《封神演义》. He had his eyes gouged out for remonstrating directly with “纣王”, the famous tyrant of the Shang Dynasty. Later, he was healed by “清虚道德真君” with golden pills, and hands grew out of his eye sockets.
 
(“清虚道德真君” was a fellow disciple of Erlang Shen’s master, similar to two professors at the same school, with Erlang Shen being the student of one professor.)
 
The large jar in the shot is a cultural relic from China’s Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods — a bronze fou with animal-head ring handles. The clay pot in her hand is a cultural relic from the Yangshao Culture (about 6,000 years ago) — the double-fish pottery jar. In ancient China, double fish symbolized blessings for a newly married couple. It is filled with rice wine, used for seasoning.
 
Finally, the food is served in a bronze basin (also from the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, more than 2,000 years ago).
 
游戏科学 is very fond of putting various cultural relics into their games.
 
The dish being made should be yellow fish crispy rice soup — fish meat and various fresh vegetables are stewed and poured over freshly fried crispy rice.
 
The bald man and the clam spirit in the video are ghosts subdued by Zhong Kui. The ghost with a huge scar on his waist is “虚耗鬼” (a ghost that wastes and consumes in vain). It is recorded in 《钟馗斩鬼传》 (The Biography of Zhong Kui Slaying Ghosts) and specializes in consuming people’s wealth and making them poor.
 
The book records that Zhong Kui killed the “木精鬼” (wood ghost) that ate livestock, the “火精鬼” (fire ghost) that burned houses, the “金精鬼” (metal ghost) that wasted property, the “水精鬼” (water ghost) that flooded fields, and the “土精鬼” (earth ghost) that ate grain.
 
These correspond respectively to “木魁”, the bald male ghost (who ignites talismans), the wounded-waist “虚耗鬼”, the clam spirit, and “肉太岁” in the video.
 
The female protagonist should be Zhong Kui’s younger sister — Zhong Meier. In ancient times, there were operas about Zhong Kui marrying off his younger sister, with all her servants being the ghosts caught by Zhong Kui.
 
The ghost standing at the back at the end is “三角兽”, an auspicious ghost that appears in various ceremonial occasions. Combined with the earlier double-fish pattern pottery jar (representing wedding blessings) and the cheerful background music, the man wearing the headgear is most likely the groom Zhong Kui found for his sister — that is, the player themselves.

Im a chemical engineer for context, and work mainly with industrial and protective coating systems for extreme environments; sulfuric acid is BY FAR more corrosive than muriatic(hydrochloric) acid in every application. You can handle hydrochloric acid without your skin being immediately injured. Of course extended exposure can cause burns, but sulfuric acid will basically start dissolving your skin instantly upon contact. Furthermore it’s significantly more hazardous to inhale as well. You can literally just walk into Home Depot and buy hydrochloric acid. It’s used often in concrete etching. Sulfuric is not as it would damage and eat away the concrete, that’s how aggressive it is. It has to be stored in high density polyethylene, especially at high concentrations. Glass can be used in smaller quantities and lesser concentrations, and carbons steel can be used only in low concentrations. For 55gal barrels it would be high density PE.

Idk man, I enjoyed the first game. 

The customization seems about the same or worse.

Graphically it doesnt look like it's improved - the textures and lighting is mostly the same.

The characters have weird proportions for facial features and I don't mean anime style. The problem is it isn't fitting the anime style or the style of their previous games.
When drawing an anime head from the chin to the top of the hair, everything usually fits in the lower half of the head, but for some reason the eyes are in the upper third.
This makes the face appear longer than it is. You'll sometimes do this for older characters, but that completely contradicts how youthful some of these characters appear [no wrinkles] creating dissonance. 

The shading is odd. In the original game the character shadows were shaded mostly with hard edges to imitate Cell-shading which is common in anime.
In the new game there are a lot more mid-tones and soft shading which results in it approaching pseudo realism or a more painterly style. 
But for me it looks more doll-like than what you'd see with characters in Arcane for example.

Part of the enjoyment in the first game was the exploration, taking inspiration from Dark Souls 1.
Linear paths that looped on themselves to create an inter-connected world that felt like exploration without being open world. 
It'll suffer from the same problem as Elden Ring as a result.
By transitioning to a more open world it leads to less curated, open areas that are big but shallow.
This is a mistake imo but I understand this is personal opinion.

The UI is completely different and reminds me more of Final Fantasy than it does Code Veins original UI design which imo felt more intuitive and easy to read.

IDK man, I'm a bit disappointed. 
It really seems like there was very little good iteration on the original other than the narrative.
Which I assume is kind of like Marvel or Dark Souls where this is taking place in an alternate universe with roughly the same setting and ideas.

It's supposedly made in UE5, but honestly I don't see the visual improvement thats supposed to bring.
Maybe it's low res textures. Maybe they didnt use the lighting fully.
Unfortunately that means we'll likely get the UE5 performance [or lack thereof] for no real benefit.

It feels like a complete departure from the original and due to the lacking visual quality, lack of innovation on character customization and UI changes it feels different but in a clunky and poorly executed way.
It looks like a game that came out in 2012 and has barely iterated on a game that came out in 2019. 
I'll maybe get it on discount, but sad to see what it became when it could have been so much better.

Battlefield 2142 had an auto correction mechanism for their vtol helicopters to prevent players from flipping over and dying. When they did the initial play tests they found it too easy to flip over and too hard to recover, so they coded in a fail-safe. It was a feature that players learned to exploit once the game launched. Letting them pull off some insane maneuvers. A whole sub culture evolved around learning to exploit a mechanic that ended up making the flying characteristics so unique to that game. It created a skill gap which rewarded those who innovated around the limits of what the gunships could do. I spent years doing dog fights within that community and I've never played another game that could replicate just how special flying those gunships felt. Bugs are sometimes the best features.
For an early access game, it's quite fun.
